gomukha
(‘mouth of the cow’)
------------------------------------------
Gomukha is the place of origin of the river गङ्गा. It is considered as a highly sacred place. Sixteen kilometres (ten miles) from Gaṅgotri (in Uttaranchal) a rivulet Devagāḍ, joins the गङ्गा. At a further distance of 6.5 kms. (4 miles) there is pine-grove. गोमुख is further up from here. Here, the river गङ्गा emerges from below a glacier. Water of the river is extremely cold. Pilgrims are advised to visit before the sun rises up, since the heat of the sun’s rays will start melting the rocks of ice and so it will be very difficult for them to walk back.
Gomukha is also the name of one of the योगासनस् described in हठयोग.
Vaiṣṇava sādhakas, generally, use an L-shaped cloth-bag to conceal their जपमाला (rosary) while doing जप. This is called ‘gomukha’.

Gomatī
------------------------------------------
Gomatī is one of the sacred rivers mentioned in the Nadīsūkta of the Ṛgveda (10.75.6). There, it is a tributary of the river Sindhū (Indus).
The modern गोमती (spelt as Gomtī) is a tributary of the river गङ्गा flowing near Lucknow (the capital of Uttar Pradesh).
According to some mythological accounts, Kauśikī, sister of विश्वामित्र, being cursed by her husband ऋचीक, became the river गोमती.
Śrī राम is said to have conducted the अश्वमेध sacrifice on the banks of this river.
The Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 169.20) says that one can get rid of one’s sins by drinking the water of this river.
The Sabhāparva of the same epic (vide 9.23) declares that the goddess गोमती, the presiding deity of the river, lives in the court of वरुण (the deity of the water principle or oceans), serving him.
Sometimes गोमती and गङ्गा are considered identical, the former being given as one of the names of the latter (Skandapurāṇa, Kāśīkhaṇḍa 29-51).
According to शातातप, a writer on the धर्मशास्त्रस् referred to by others, गोमती is a type of Vedic मन्त्र used in prāyaścittas or expiations, especially for killing a cow.

Gommaṭeśvara
(‘lord of Cupid’, ‘lord of beauty’)
------------------------------------------
Establishing the images of great persons in public places seems to be a natural trait of human beings in almost all the cultures and civilisations of the world. But in India, where religion gets precedence over all other aspects of life, the images of gods and saints are seen carved out or put up everywhere, especially in places of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
One of the images of Jaina tradition more frequently found is that of Gomma-ṭeśvara (also spelt as ‘Gomaṭeśvara’), mostly in the Karnataka State.
गोम्मटेश्वर at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa">Śrī गोम्मटेश्वर at ŚravaṇabeḷagoḷaGommaṭeśvara’s earlier name was Bāhubali. He was the last son of Vṛṣabha-nātha, the first of the Tīrthaṅkaras (founders of जैनिस्म्). After distributing his kingdom among his children, Vṛṣabha-nātha retired for तपस्. भरत, the eldest son, started on an invasion tour and conquered all the kings except his own brothers. When challenged, they too renounced the world and retired for तपस्, abdicating their kingdoms in his favour. However, Bāhubali, the youngest of the brothers, refused to oblige. When भरत fought a duel with him, he was defeated. But Bāhubali, eventhough he was the victor, refused to be the emperor and started performing severe तपस् standing in the same place. He attained enlightenment very soon. भरत established his image in Paudanapura (near उज्जयिनी in Madhya Pradesh).
There are quite a few images of गोम्मटेश्वर or Bāhubali in India, most of them being in the Karnataka State. The relief figure, about 2 1/4 metres (7 1/2 ft.) high found in a Jaina cave of Bādāmī (in Karnataka) is the earliest among these (7th cent. A. D.). There is another in the Meṇada-basadi of ऐहोऌए (Bijapur district of Karnataka) probably belonging to the period A.

.
Some गोम्मटेश्वर icons are found in the Jaina caves of एल्लोर (in Maharashtra) also.
By far, the biggest and the most well-known of all these images is the one on the hillock in Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa (Hasan district of Karnataka). It has been sculptured out of a single stone on a small hillock. Cāmuṇḍarāya, the prime minister of the king Rācamalla of the Gaṅga dynasty is said to have got it made during the period A.

-983. It is 17.4 metres (58 ft.) high. There is a beautiful, but almost imperceptible, smile on his face. The body is naked and covered with wild creepers here and there.
Other images of गोम्मटेश्वर are at Kārkaḷa (12.5 metres or 41.5 ft.), Veṇūr (10.5 metres or 35 ft.), Dharmasthaḷa (11.7 metres or 39 ft.), Gomaṭagiri (5.4 metres or 18 ft.) and Bastihaḷḷi (5.4 metres or 18 ft.). All these are in the Karnataka State only.
The image at Kārkaḷa was established by Vīrapāṇḍya in A.
and the one at Veṇūr by Timmaṇṇa Ajila in A.
. The Dharmasthaḷa image was installed very recently, in 1973.

Gomukha-prasava-śānti
------------------------------------------
Belief in astrological phenomena and predictions based on the होरोस्चोपे is very strong in the Hindu society even today. The Āśleṣa नक्षत्र (the स्तर्स् comprising eta, sigma, delta, epsilon, rho and zeta hydrae) is considered rākṣasa or demoniac in nature and hence birth under it is considered inauspicious for the baby. To ward off the evil effects the गोमुख prasava-śānti is performed by the parents. The whole rite is aimed at making the baby to be ‘reborn’ (prasava) from the mouth of a cow (gomukha) at an auspicious moment.
Keeping the new-born baby in a winnowing basket covered with a piece of cloth, bringing the basket near the mouth of a cow (as if it is new born from the cow’s mouth), bathing it with the milk of the cow, handing it over to the ड़थेर् and then to the मोथेर्, all the while chanting appropriate Vedic mantras—these are some of the steps involved in the rite.
